content: Serum sickness is an immune system reaction that mimics an allergic response. It occurs when the body reacts to certain medications, injected proteins used for immune conditions, or antiserum, which is the antibody-containing liquid portion of blood that helps protect against infections or toxins. Symptoms of Serum Sickness: However, in individuals who have been previously exposed to the substance, symptoms may develop within 1 to 3 days. Causes of Serum Sickness: Plasma, the clear fluid component of blood, contains proteins such as antibodies that are part of the immune system's defense against infections. Antiserum is derived from the plasma of individuals or animals with immunity to a specific infection or toxin. In serum sickness, the immune system mistakenly identifies a protein in the antiserum as a harmful antigen. This triggers an inappropriate immune response, leading to the formation of immune complexes. These complexes cause inflammation and other symptoms. Certain medications, such as penicillin, cefaclor, and sulfa drugs, can also induce a similar reaction. Injected proteins, such as antithymocyte globulin (used for organ transplant rejection) and rituximab (used for immune disorders and cancers), as well as blood products, can also trigger serum sickness. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if symptoms of serum sickness develop within four weeks of receiving medication or antiserum. Diagnosis: Enlarged and tender lymph nodes may be present. Urine tests may reveal blood or protein. Blood tests may detect immune complexes or signs of blood vessel inflammation. Treatment Options: Corticosteroid creams or ointments, as well as other soothing skin treatments, can alleviate itching and rash. Antihistamines may reduce the duration of illness and relieve rash and itching. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, can help with joint pain. Oral corticosteroids, such as prednisone, may be prescribed for severe cases. The medication or antiserum causing the reaction should be discontinued, and future use of the same substance should be avoided. Prognosis: Symptoms of serum sickness usually resolve within a few days. Possible Complications: If the causative drug or antiserum is used again, there is a high risk of experiencing another similar reaction. Potential complications include: Anaphylactic shock, a severe and life-threatening reaction Inflammation of blood vessels Swelling of the face, arms, and legs Prevention: There is no definitive way to prevent serum sickness. Individuals who have experienced serum sickness, anaphylactic shock, or drug allergies should avoid future use of the causative antiserum or medication.
